description: We are a team of 6 members united by one goal, which is to provide the highest levels of safety for astronauts on long missions. An immediate emergency protection and response system aims to protect astronauts during external missions, as the team addresses the risk of sudden pressure release resulting from a split in the space helmet.
summary:
"ASTRA" is an intelligent system designed to monitor the health of astronauts. We created it to help track and understand their well-being throughout space missions. The idea began with a straightforward question: how can an astronaut’s health be monitored when they are far from Earth and do not always have access to immediate medical care?

To meet this need, we aimed to develop a system that extends beyond simple data gathering. ASTRA structures health information, evaluates how it changes over time, detects possible warning signs, and displays the results in a format that is easy to understand. We consider this system essential: monitoring an astronaut’s health is not limited to knowing their present condition—it also involves recognizing emerging changes early and interpreting what they indicate. Our objective is to make health monitoring more intelligent, more transparent, and more useful for upcoming space missions.
details:
"ASTRA" is a software prototype created to make the monitoring of astronaut health more structured and more intelligent.

We built "ASTRA" as a platform that brings together multiple health-monitoring functions in one place. Instead of merely showing raw figures, the system converts the available health data into actionable information, enabling users to gain a clearer understanding of an astronaut’s health condition.

The platform comprises several essential components:

1. Digital Astronaut Health Profile: Collects and organizes an astronaut’s health information into a single unified file. 2. "ASTRA" Intelligent Engine: Analyzes available health data to generate meaningful insights. 3. Health Trend Forecasting: Reviews health data across time to predict possible future trends. 4. Contextual Health Alerts: Draws attention to potential health issues while also clarifying the reasoning behind each alert. 5. Mission Simulation Lab: Lets users examine different health-monitoring scenarios within simulated missions. 6. Real-Time Monitoring Architecture: Establishes a basis for incorporating physical health-monitoring hardware in subsequent versions. 7. Automated Health Reports: Produces structured reports derived from health data. 8. Crew Health Overview: Offers a consolidated summary of health information for every crew member. 9. Mission Comparison: Allows users to compare different mission scenarios.10. “ASTRA” AI Assistant: An interactive assistant designed to facilitate communication in both Arabic and English through text and voice. The project was developed using the Python programming language, and the Streamlit framework was used to build the web application. We used the Pandas library for data organization and processing, and the Plotly library to produce interactive visualizations, along with additional software libraries to enable voice interaction. To strengthen the intelligent assistant’s capabilities, the Google Gemini API has been integrated.

The current version functions as a software prototype; some of its features depend on experimental or simulated data, and physical monitoring hardware has not yet been incorporated or evaluated under real spaceflight conditions.

Our main objective is to transform ASTRA from a software prototype into a full-fledged platform for monitoring astronaut health. In the next phase, we plan to develop the required physical hardware, connect it with the software, test sensor readings in real-world settings, and improve the system through ongoing validation and development. What makes ASTRA especially important to us is its underlying core concept: we intend to move beyond merely recording health indicators—we want to make these metrics easier to understand and more actionable, so we can better support astronauts during their missions.
